claims.text: A single in-situ laser re-melting pass should be applied immediately after each deposited LPBF layer.
Laser power, scan speed, and delay time for the re-melting pass can be dynamically optimized by a real-time machine-learning control system.
Layer-wise laser re-melting with real-time control will reduce steep local thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients will produce a more uniform melt pool and more homogeneous re-solidification.
The secondary laser pass will heal porosity and incomplete-fusion defects.
The secondary laser pass will produce smoother layer interfaces.
Re-heating the just-deposited layer will decrease rapid temperature fluctuations and residual stresses.
Controlled re-solidification after re-melting will refine the microstructure.
Defect healing, residual-stress reduction, and microstructural refinement will improve dimensional fidelity.
Defect healing, residual-stress reduction, and microstructural refinement will improve mechanical properties.
Conventional LPBF high-entropy-alloy components can contain fabrication-induced defects.
Conventional LPBF high-entropy-alloy components exhibit uneven thermal gradients, residual stresses, rough layer interfaces, porosity, and lack of fusion.
The intervention will reduce defect volume fraction by approximately 40% relative to conventional LPBF.
The intervention will improve yield strength and ultimate tensile strength by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional LPBF.
The intervention will achieve tighter dimensional tolerances than conventional LPBF.
At high or extreme energy densities, other defect modes can attenuate or offset process improvements.
Alloys with atypical thermal properties may obtain less benefit from the re-melting intervention.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on alloy composition, machine-learning control tuning, and interactions with other processing variables.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes re-solidification as defect-free, implying elimination of defects, whereas the quantitative prediction is only an approximately 40% reduction in defect volume fraction.
